---
title: "Step 2 · Quantifying AMR with ResScan"
subtitle: "Map the clean reads against CARD and report resistance per bacterial cell — one sample, then all 36."
---

Now the clean reads meet the resistance database. **ResScan** maps each sample
against [CARD](https://card.mcmaster.ca/) to find AMR genes, *and* against a set of
universal single-copy bacterial genes to estimate how many bacterial cells were
there — then divides one by the other to report **RPKPMC**, its preferred default
metric: resistance-gene copies *per bacterial cell*.

We'll do it twice: **one sample by hand** to see the shape of the output, then
**all 36 at once** in batch mode.

```bash
mamba activate resscan-env
```

::: {.callout-note}
## A reminder about depth
These are 10,000-read samples — a keyhole view. Your per-sample tables will be
**sparse, maybe empty**, and that's completely fine: the goal here is to run the tool
correctly. Real, populated results come from the full data (used in Step 3).
:::

## 2a · One sample

Give ResScan the sample's two vanished mate files (comma-separated), an output
prefix, some threads, and the CARD database you built in Setup:

```bash
mkdir -p resscan_single
resscan -i vanished/vanished_reads/SRR10842836_1.fastq.gz,vanished/vanished_reads/SRR10842836_2.fastq.gz \
        -o resscan_single/SRR10842836 \
        -t 4 \
        --card resscan_CARD_v4.0.1
```

When it finishes, look at what it produced:

```bash
ls resscan_single/
```

The key file is `SRR10842836_homscan.tsv` in the `SRR10842836` folder — one row per
detected AMR gene, with all the normalised metrics (including the default `RPKPMC`)
as columns. There's also a
VarScan table for point-mutation resistance and interactive HTML coverage plots.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What are all these files, columns, and metrics?
The [output reference](output-reference.qmd) breaks down every file ResScan writes,
what each column means, how to decode the metric names, and the one label worth
understanding up front — `multiple`. Worth a look before you dive into the numbers.
:::

That's one sample. Doing it 36 times by hand would be tedious and error-prone — so
ResScan ships a batch mode.

## 2b · All 36 at once (batch mode)

`resscan_batch` runs ResScan across every sample listed in a **samplesheet** — a
plain CSV that is both the batch's *input* and a durable *record* of exactly what
you ran (keep it with your results). Each line is one sample: its name, then its
read file(s). We ship one ready to go — take a look:

```bash
head -3 data/samplesheet.csv
```

```default
SRR10842836,vanished/vanished_reads/SRR10842836_1.fastq.gz,vanished/vanished_reads/SRR10842836_2.fastq.gz
SRR10842837,vanished/vanished_reads/SRR10842837_1.fastq.gz,vanished/vanished_reads/SRR10842837_2.fastq.gz
...
```

Each line is `sample_id,R1,R2`. Commas separate a run's mates; **semicolons
separate runs** — so a sample sequenced across two runs goes on one line as
`SAMPLE,run1_R1,run1_R2;run2_R1,run2_R2`.

::: {.callout-note}
## List *all* of a sample's reads together
Pooling every run for a sample is what makes the **lateral coverage** metric
meaningful — a gene's coverage along its length is only correct when the full set of
that sample's reads is considered at once. (This is the same `-i` format `resscan`
uses for a single sample — see the ResScan README.)
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Paths are relative to where you launch.** The paths above are relative to your
working directory (this repo's root, where the `vanished/` folder from Step 1 lives);
`resscan_batch` resolves them for you. Absolute paths work too.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Prefer to build your own samplesheet?
The helper `create_samplesheet_from_mapping` stamps a samplesheet out of a simple
`sample_id,file_prefix` mapping — e.g.

```bash
create_samplesheet_from_mapping --mapping data/sampleid2fileprefix.csv \
    --fastq-dir vanished/vanished_reads --out samplesheet.csv
```

Or just write the CSV by hand in the format above. Either way, the batch only ever
reads the samplesheet.
:::

Now run the whole batch on the shipped samplesheet. `--parallel` sets how many
samples run at once and `--threads` how many cores each gets — tune both to your
machine:

```bash
resscan_batch \
    --samplesheet data/samplesheet.csv \
    --card resscan_CARD_v4.0.1 \
    --out SinkReplacementBatch \
    --parallel 4 \
    --threads 2
```

```default
 N E X T F L O W   ~  version 26.04.x
executor >  local

[..] RESSCAN (SRR10842854) [100%] 36 of 36 ✔

--- Batch Run Complete ---
Status:  SUCCESS
```

## 2c · Consolidate into one set of tables

Batch mode writes a folder *per sample*. `resscan_aggregate` pivots them into
wide, analysis-ready tables — one file per metric, samples as columns:

```bash
resscan_aggregate \
    -s data/samplesheet.csv \
    -i SinkReplacementBatch \
    -o SinkReplacementBatchReports \
    -p SR
```

```bash
ls SinkReplacementBatchReports/ | head
```

You'll get files like `SR_homscan_RPKPMC.tsv`, `SR_homscan_RPKM.tsv`,
`SR_varscan_RPKPMC.tsv`, … — the exact shape the analysis uses. (On this subset
they'll be sparse; the **full-depth** versions are already in `data/reports_full/`,
which Step 3 uses.)

## Tidy up

```bash
rm -rf work .nextflow*
mamba deactivate
```

You've quantified AMR the recommended way. Next, get to know the output in the
[**output reference**](output-reference.qmd), or head straight to **Step 3 · Analysis**.
